Restaurant review: The Bull at Broughton, North Yorkshire | Restaurants

Lancashire is: Just William; Freddie Flintoff; Blackpool; Eccles cakes; Peter Kay, Victoria Wood; Frank Evans (who? the Lancashire matador, of course); Paul Heathcote; black pudding and hot pies; and where "women die of love", according to Honoré de Balzac (according to Charles Nevin, to whom I am indebted for much of the above).

Yorkshire is: Wuthering Heights; Geoffrey Boycott; Harrogate; Alan Titchmarsh; parkin; Richard Whiteley; Roy Hattersley; Marco Pierre White; Terry's chocolates and Yorkshire pudding; and David Hockney. As someone once said, "You can always tell a Yorkshireman... but you can't tell him much."

And now Lancashire has invaded Yorkshire. And not before time, some might say. Those doughty Lancastrians, Nigel Howarth and Craig Bancroft, his partner in various gastropub ventures in Lancashire, as well as in the more polished Northcote Manor, have taken over The Bull at Broughton.

The hallmark of Howarth/Bancroft establishments is that they are less gastropubs in the conventional sense, or what has come to be the conventional sense (ie more restaurant than boozer), and more like brasserie-pubs. You can get good beer – I can strongly recommend the Dark Horse Hetton Pale Ale and the raspberry-flavoured Saltaire Raspberry Blonde with which I eased down my supper – or you can munch your way through some serious grub, too.

That doesn't mean serious in the sense of overwrought, fine dining stuff. It's serious in that Howarth and co give serious thought to the kind of food we like to eat. On the back of the menu is a map marking 27 of the producers supplying The Bull – most are clustered around Skipton, three miles down the road. And you'll find those same suppliers all over the menu proper – Yellinson Farm goat's cheese, Bolton Abbey lamb, Charles Ashridge's saddleback pork, Yoadwarth Mill smoked salmon, Dales raspberries.

This sense of locality is carried through into the dishes themselves. Of course there's Yorkshire pudding (with slow-cooked oxtail bits, gravy and Mrs Carr's raspberry vinegar), Barnsley chop, Yorkshire Dales ribeye bloomer sandwich, frumenty, sticky parkin and Yorkshire curd tart. Oh, and the fish, scampi and chips are fried in beef dripping. But this isn't just a dutiful tour though the great traditions of the Yorkshire kitchen. Howarth knows when to leave well alone and when to give a dish a contemporary nudge.

I started off with wild rabbit faggots, roast courgette purée and tomato juices – eight two-bite balls of improbably intense rabbit mince, a soothing, rough purée of courgettes and a chirpily fresh tomato sauce with a nip of chilli – a Yorkshire portion, too, and for only £5.50. The quantity alone made the price daft, but the quality showed up the pedestrian nature of much of what passes for gastropub food these days. Even such a hoary favourite as scampi and chips has had a discrete polish. The scampi are proper, sweet-tailed things inside a light, crisp, utterly British beer batter, and they come in a smart wooden bowl rather than a basket. There's a lemon and black pepper mayo to dip them into and a pile of chips. I don't know what makes beef dripping the ideal medium for chips, but it is. Even Heston Blumenthal's rightly lauded triple-cooked chips come off second best to the dripping-fried variety, which have a dulcet note, a depth of flavour, a whisper of meatiness, that lifts them from vehicles for ketchup to sublime gastronomic experiences in their own right.

And for pudding, frumenty, an old Yorkshire combination of cracked wheat, spelt or some such, creamy substances and cracking raspberries.

As the light filtered through the windows and shadows began to stretch across the stone-flagged floor, families of all ages relaxed, ate and chatted. That's the Bull for you – decent, cheerful, fun, good value, with terrific grub. A bit of Yorkshire magic… thanks to some Lancastrians.

The Bull


The Bull at Broughton has long been one of Yorkshire's landmark pubs...famous as much for its hospitality as it is for its beautiful location. Enjoy regional Cask Ales and an award winning wine list specially chosen by leading wine expert, Craig Bancroft. The Bull is full of atmosphere, character and charm, but above all its relaxing, with al fresco dining in the summer and crackling log fires in the winter.
